recall_prompt: Say how you would prove that 10 C 3 plus 10 C 6 equals 11 C 4.
insider_note: Pascal needs lower numbers one apart, so the one required move is ¹⁰C₆ = ¹⁰C₄. After it the identity gives ¹¹C₄ in one line — and a prove-that question ends at "= R.H.S.", not at the identity.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Rewrite ¹⁰C₆ as ¹⁰C₄
steps.margin_note: First mark. ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ, so ¹⁰C₆ = ¹⁰C₄. Now the two lower numbers differ by one.
steps.memory_tip: 3 and 6 are not one apart. Rewrite ¹⁰C₆ as ¹⁰C₄ so Pascal can be used.

recall.must_convey: That 10 C 6 is rewritten as 10 C 4 using n C r equals n C n minus r, so the left side is 10 C 3 plus 10 C 4.
accept: ten C six is ten C four because n C r equals n C n minus r, so the left side is ten C three plus ten C four
change ten C six to ten C four first
rewrite ten C six as ten C ten minus six which is ten C four
ten C six ni ten C four ga rayali
use the complement rule on ten C six

steps.why: Pascal's identity needs two lower numbers one apart. 3 and 6 are not; 3 and 4 are. The rewrite is what makes the identity usable.
common_mistakes: Applying Pascal directly to ¹⁰C₃ + ¹⁰C₆ — the lower numbers must differ by one.
Rewriting ¹⁰C₃ as ¹⁰C₇ instead — ¹⁰C₇ + ¹⁰C₆ = ¹¹C₇ = ¹¹C₄ reaches the same answer, but it needs the complement rule a second time at the end.

steps.label: Apply ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₊₁ = ⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾Cᵣ₊₁
steps.margin_note: Second mark. With n = 10 and r = 3 the identity gives ¹¹C₄, which is the right-hand side.
steps.memory_tip: ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₊₁ = ⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾Cᵣ₊₁ with n = 10, r = 3 gives ¹¹C₄. End at '= R.H.S.'.

recall.must_convey: That Pascal's identity n C r plus n C r plus 1 equals n plus 1 C r plus 1 gives 11 C 4, the right-hand side.
accept: n C r plus n C r plus one is n plus one C r plus one so ten C three plus ten C four is eleven C four which is the right hand side
apply Pascal to get eleven C four
ten C three plus ten C four equals eleven C four, proved
Pascal identity tho eleven C four vasthundi, R H S
the sum of the two is eleven C four
heard_as: n plus one C r plus one

steps.why: Pascal's identity is the statement that choosing r + 1 from n + 1 either uses a fixed item or does not. Naming it, with its n and r, is what turns two lines into a proof.
common_mistakes: Writing the identity as ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₊₁ = ⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾Cᵣ, with the wrong lower number on the right.
Not ending with "= R.H.S." on a "prove that" question.
